p: On the first Saturday in April, Graham ran Kit's first full practice test at the kitchen table, eleven blocks in the order and the minutes the real test uses. He called time at the end of every block and said nothing else all morning.

In Word Knowledge she hit the word dissemble, to put on a false front, and knew it for her own seven years. When a math problem stalled her, she guessed, marked it and moved on. In Physical Science, the subject Graham has taught for years and she'd never once asked him about, she knew from the water plant that the pressure at the bottom of a tank depends on its depth, not its width.

That night she put her 2019 score sheet on the kitchen table and told Graham herself. Her Pilot score had been nineteen. When Boyd asked her to stay for an inspection, she'd said yes, because yes meant she never had to say nineteen to Graham, and she'd let Boyd's request be the reason. Graham said he'd made his peace with the pilot slot back in January. What he couldn't get past was that she'd let him think it was Boyd for seven years. She didn't defend it. She said, I did, and stayed at the table.

Then he took her out to the garage and folded back a corner of the tarp over the crib. Two springs ago he'd asked her whether this was the year they'd try for a baby, and she'd said after. He asked her not to hand him another after. She told him she didn't know yet, that she wanted to fly, and that she wasn't going to say after to make the night easier. He said okay.

On Sunday she called her mother and asked for an hour at her table on Sunday, April 11, when drill lets out at four, to tell her something from 2019 in person. Rhonda said she'd make a roast. On Tuesday she told Vern that Graham knew, and he said, that's one. On Wednesday Graham kept the lab date he'd put on the whiteboard in February. In Room 114 he told her his sophomores bring him failing tests every week, and she could have brought him a nineteen. Then he taught her density, hydraulics and circuits, careful and kind, and he didn't say her name all afternoon.

Friday morning she came home from a night shift to her practice test scored in red. His only note said AR, twenty one of twenty five, Good. Her weakest blocks for the Pilot composite were Instrument Comprehension and Aviation Information, the airplane from the inside. She stuck his note on the fold of her 2019 sheet, so it would come out of her pocket first. Then she wrote him a note of her own and stuck it on the coffee maker. PS, thirteen of twenty. Will you teach me the seven?

Saturday, April 10, ten to four in the morning. The launch board was where it always was, on the wall by the coffee, and two two eight was on it for eight thirty. Beside it, in Boyd's grease pencil from February, DARROW. Same board as March. In March the thing that had to come off before the jet went anywhere had been a tire.
The light was on in Boyd's office. It was always on by now. She could see the top of his head over the partition and the steam off his cup.

Her note had been gone from the coffee maker when she woke up Friday afternoon. Nothing in its place. At supper Graham had told her about a kid in third period who'd wired a doorbell backward, and he'd laughed, and he hadn't said one word about the seven. She hadn't asked. It was his to answer.
The sheet was in her coat, folded, with his yellow note on the outside. She didn't take it out. Boyd wouldn't need paper. She'd ask him for ten minutes once the jet was gone.

At twenty past four she and Fisk walked two two eight with their flashlights, nose to tail, the way they did every launch. He'd brought her a coffee from the machine, which he did now on drill mornings without saying why.
He'd slept. She could tell from how he walked, and from his eyes, and from the fact that he'd remembered both gloves. He didn't say how, and she didn't ask.

Under the left wing he stopped and put his light on the leading edge, the long rounded front of it, wet with dew. Boom operator told me Thursday a wing can stall with its nose pointed straight at the ground. I told him that's when you've got the most speed. He said look it up, Airman. I didn't look it up.

She put her own light up beside his. It's the angle to the air, she told him. Tip the front of a wing up into the air coming at it far enough, and the air can't stay on top. It lets go, and the lift goes with it. Nose high, nose low, fast or slow. Pull hard out of a dive and you can get there with the nose pointed at a cornfield. Fisk stood with his light on the wing like it might do it right then. Guess I owe him a coffee. Two. He's a boom operator.

That's it, the critical angle of attack, measured against the relative wind. Every wing has one, and past it the air peels off the top and the lift falls away. Where the nose points doesn't decide it, and the speed doesn't by itself either. So any attitude, any airspeed, any power setting. The fix is less angle. My first year on tankers a boom operator told me the same thing, and I argued with him too, and it cost me a dollar.
Two two eight came off the ground at eight thirty one and turned out over the river. Kit watched it until it was a dot, then walked to the office.

Boyd had a launch sheet in one hand and his cup in the other. The picture of him at twenty by the nose gear was still taped to the side of his monitor, curling at the corners. She shut the door behind her. He looked at it, and then at her.
That's twice this year you've shut my door, Darrow. He set the cup down on the inbox, where the routing slip had sat for almost four weeks in January. Go ahead.

It wasn't the inspection, Sergeant Boyd. My Pilot score came back nineteen that fall, and it has to be twenty five. You asked me to stay, and I said yes so I'd never have to say nineteen on this ramp. Every time a board went up and you looked at me like you owed me, I let you pay. She didn't sit down. She didn't take the sheet out of her coat. She said it standing up, the way you'd report a write up.

For a while Boyd didn't say anything. He picked up the cup and didn't drink from it. Then he laughed, once, through his nose, and put his hand flat over his eyes, the way a man does when the bill he's been paying turns out to be somebody else's.
Seven years. Every time a board went up on that corkboard, I'd look at you and think, there's the one I cost. And you let me.

He put the cup down. You want to know why your slip sat under that cup? When these jets go, I go. Thirty one years on this airplane. I built you to stay. You were the one thing on this ramp I wasn't going to have to hand back.
And DARROW on every launch? Both. Keeping you close. And putting you in front of her every Saturday so she'd see what she'd be getting.

I'm sorry you carried it. I let you. And I still want to go. Boyd looked at her for a long time, long enough for the phone on his desk to ring and quit. Yeah. I know you do. That's the part I'm mad about. He picked up the launch sheet again. Go on. Your jet's back at one.
At a quarter to twelve she walked to the heritage room on her lunch. Vern was at the slate table with a paper sack and a thermos. He looked up.

She sat down across from him and didn't say anything. He looked at her a while. Then he got up, took the keys off his belt, and got the case open on the first try this time. Out from under the glass came the attitude indicator. Corbin's altimeter stayed put, its needles on field elevation. The old dial went on the table between them. A crack in the glass at seven o'clock, and a little white airplane painted across the middle.

It's dead. No gyro spinning in there, so the card just hangs where it falls. That's fine. I'll draw you the live one. He went to the slate board on the wall, the one older than he was, and drew with a stub of chalk out of his shirt pocket. A circle. A little airplane across the middle with its wings straight out. Then the horizon line, sky over it and ground under. The line went up over the little airplane, uphill to the right. The grade on the river road, about.

Two looks. Line over the nose. Nose down. Diving. Wings next. Uphill to the right meant the right end was the high end. Right wing low. Banked right. Vern rubbed it out with the side of his fist and drew another before she could feel good about it.

Pitch first, then bank. Horizon over the little airplane, nose under it, diving. For the bank, look at which end of the line is higher. Line's high on the right, so the right wing's the low one. Right bank, and on a real dial the pointer would sit off zero to the right to back you up. That took you about six seconds. You'd have had six to spare, and you'll want them for the ones that point at you.
On the shelf by the case was a gray desk model of a tanker on a stand, missing its boom, with a tag on it in Patrice's printing that said PLEASE DO NOT HANDLE. Vern handled it.
On the test you're always standing south of it, at its height, looking north. I'm north. East is your right. He held the model out across the table at his eye level, nose pointed straight at her.
Then he tipped it. The wing on her left side went down, the wing on her right came up. Nose still at her, level.
Heading and bank, Sergeant. Twelve seconds.

Nose at her, so south. Then she put herself in the seat, facing her own chair. From in there, the low wing was on the right hand. Banked right. Vern set the model back on its stand, nose to the wall, the way Patrice liked it.

Nose toward you is heading south. Then sit in the seat. Facing you, the airplane's right wing is on your left, so a dip on your left is a right bank. That's the one people miss most, and the test knows it. Slow down on the nose toward you pictures. They're worth the extra two seconds.
At twenty past twelve she put her coat back on. Vern was screwing the lid onto his thermos.

She'd said one thing this morning she'd held for seven years. This one she'd held since January, at a diner counter, where she'd nearly asked him and hadn't. She'd sat at his kitchen table every Tuesday since, with a box in the den with 2001 on the end of it, and hadn't. She'd been seven that summer.
She knew three things about family day. A navigator's seat, too big for her. A man's voice. A hand pointing up at the ceiling. She didn't know which jet, and she didn't know the man's face.
She stood by the case with her coat on and looked up at the ceiling tiles, which had nothing in them.

Were you on family day in 2001? I sat in a navigator's seat that summer. I was seven. I don't know whose jet it was. Vern set the thermos down. He held still the way he did when the egg timer was about to go, and it wasn't anywhere near going. June. We had one that June. He looked at the case, not at her. It's in the box. It's the one I haven't picked. I'll bring it tomorrow.

She thought about June on the walk back and made herself stop. Two two eight came home at ten past one. Kit and Fisk drove out to meet it in the truck, the long way around on the perimeter road, because the short way crossed the alternate runway and nobody had called the tower for it.

The road ran beside a taxiway for a stretch. Where the taxiway met the alternate runway there were four yellow lines across the concrete, two solid and two dashed, and beside them a sign on two little legs. Red, with white numbers on it, 17-35.
I drive past that every drill. Red means stop, I figure, and then you just go?

Red with white letters was an order, she told him. A runway holding position sign. The runway's just past it, 17 at one end and 35 at the other, and you don't put a tire over the solid lines till the tower says so. Truck or airplane, same rule. Fisk turned in his seat to watch it go by. So, stop and wait. Not stop and go. He said it again under his breath, the way he'd say a torque value.

Red with white lettering is a mandatory sign. This one's a runway holding position sign, with the runway's numbers on it, right at the hold line. Stop on the solid side of those four lines and don't cross without a clearance. Black with yellow letters tells you where you are. Yellow with black letters and an arrow says which way to go. You know what kind of sign it is from the color before you've read a word, and on a dark ramp in the rain the color's what you can see.

At three there was an engine run. Number two had come home with a write up on its oil pressure, a flicker in the climb, and the specialists wanted it run at power once they'd been through it. Kit took the left seat. Fisk was on the long interphone cord out by the engine, where he could see it.

She ran the checklist the way she'd run it a hundred times, brakes set, chocks in, clearance from the tower on the radio. Number two came up to power, and the jet leaned into the chocks and stayed put.

Then, with the gauges steady and nothing to do but watch them, she did something she'd never done in eleven years in that seat. She looked at the rest of the panel the way a pilot would. The attitude display in front of her, the little airplane sitting on the horizon line, wings level, nose a hair above, the way the jet sat on its gear on this end of the ramp. Level flight, if it had been flying. The heading read 320. Northwest and a little more. The direction she'd be pointed, if anybody ever let her off these brakes. At eight thirty one, two two eight had gone off the end of this runway and turned right for the river, out to 050. Vern had sat sideways behind that turn for twenty years and never once seen it from here.
She thought of Vern's card from the lesson, three degrees a second, all the way around in two minutes.

Forty degrees from 320 up to north. Fifty more past north to 050. Ninety, all told. At three degrees a second that was thirty seconds. She had it before number two's oil pressure needle had moved. Then the specialist's voice came over the interphone, asking for idle, and she brought it back.

Count the turn in two pieces when it crosses north. From 320 to 360 is 40, and from 000 to 050 is 50, so 90 in all. At three degrees a second, 90 divided by 3 is thirty seconds. Same answer as a quarter of the two minute circle. The miss is subtracting the headings straight, 320 less 50, and turning the long way.
Saturday night Graham had been at the kitchen table with a pack of blank index cards and his black marker. When she came in he turned the stack face down and asked how Boyd took it.

Sunday at seven a medevac helicopter came in low over the river and set down on the pad on the civil side, by the terminal. A white van was already there with its back doors open, and two people in blue stood well off to one side holding their caps on. Fisk stopped with a tow bar in his hands. The helicopter hung there a few feet up with its nose down a little, and the grass along the pad went flat and silver. Then it slid forward across the concrete, with nothing pushing it either of them could see, and sat down.
Fisk watched the blades wind down. Kemp says if you get it you're gone a year, easy. Who's on her then? Kit didn't answer that one. It wasn't hers to answer yet. He looked back at the pad.
How's it go forward? There's no prop.

She'd seen the nose dip before it went. The stick. Cyclic. He leans it, the whole spinning thing up top leans with it, and some of the lift pulls him forward. Fisk chewed on that, tow bar still in his hands. Like leaning into a walk. Close enough for a Sunday.

The cyclic. Lean the stick and the rotor disc leans, because each blade takes a little more bite on one side of the circle than the other. Leaned forward, part of the lift pulls forward. The collective's up and down. The pedals point the nose. I learned that hollering back and forth with a Guard pilot over the river in '93. I caught about half of what he said, and that half was the cyclic.
At noon he was at the slate table again, with no sack and no thermos. He had a log in front of him, folded once and squared to the edge of the table.
He'd said he'd bring it. He slid it across to her and kept two fingers on it a second before he let go.
She unfolded it. His capitals, the same square hand as every other one, a little bigger, as if he'd been writing it on his knee.

Nine June, oh one. Family day. Two two eight on static, north ramp. Nav seat open ten to fifteen hundred. Thirty some kids. One girl about seven would not get out. Asked what the hole in the ceiling is for. Told her that's where the stars come in. Asked me which seat is the best one. Told her this one. She did not believe me.
Two two eight. She read it again. She looked up, and he was looking at the case, the way he had yesterday.

I don't know yet. My mother's got a picture on her fridge from that day. I'll know by supper, and I'll call you either way. Vern nodded once. He refolded the log along its old crease and pushed it back across to her. Keep it on you. She put it in her coat, on top of everything else in there.
At half past three, with the shop half closed down for release, Boyd called her into his office. The door was already shut when she got there. He opened it for her and shut it again.

There was a yellow legal pad on the desk, one page written on in pencil, in the square printing he'd used on her training records when she was twenty one. The pencil was a carpenter's pencil, flat, sharpened on the bench grinder. She'd never seen him write anything longer than a forms entry.

For your package. I did it at my kitchen table last night. My wife says it's fine. She'd say that. He put one thick finger on a word near the bottom. Before I read it to you. You're the one studying words. I wrote that I recommend you unequivocally. Does that mean what I think it means?
It means no doubt in it. No but. Boyd nodded slowly, the way he did when a torque value came out where he'd expected. Then it stays.
He read it to her once, standing at the desk, the pad held out at arm's length because he wouldn't wear his glasses in front of her. Halfway into the first line he stopped and looked up.
Look at me, Darrow. Not the floor. She looked at him, and he read the rest of it to her face.

To the selection board. I have been on the KC-135 since 1996, and I have been Staff Sergeant Katherine Darrow's supervisor since she was twenty one. She is the best crew chief I have trained. In March she held a jet the forms said was ready, and she was right. She tells the truth when it costs her. That is the thing I would want in the seat. I recommend her unequivocally. Seven years ago I asked her to stay, and she did. I am not asking again. Arlen Boyd, Master Sergeant.

He signed it with the carpenter's pencil, pressed hard enough to go through, the way he'd signed her slip. He tore it off the pad. Then he said the other thing to the window. Your name stays under that window till you fly it. If the new jets come first, I'll paint it on one of them myself.
Vern had told her in February that the board could get that one from Boyd.
At ten after four she pulled up at her mother's across the river. Rhonda had the roast on, and the kitchen windows were steamed, and she'd set two places at the table where Kit had done her homework.

They ate first. Then Kit put her fork down and told her. The nineteen. The yes. Boyd, yesterday, with his door shut. The letter, an hour ago. Rhonda listened with her hands around her coffee, and when it was over she said Kitty, once. I've been bragging on a girl who stayed for her people. I'll brag on this one now. You can argue with me about it some other night.
The family day picture was where it had been since 2001, on the freezer door, under the dentist magnet. April's lunch menu was clipped over the top half. Taco Tuesday. Kit got up and unclipped it.

She was seven in it, in a seat too big for her, in a green T shirt, looking up. A man's arm came in from the edge of the picture, cut off at the shoulder by her mother's camera, and his hand pointed at a small round fitting in the ceiling. On the hand was a ring. Gold, with a stone, worn thin on one side. She'd shaken that hand at the Riverside in January.

Her mother watched her from the sink. You cried from the gate to the bridge that day. I asked what hurt, and you said nothing hurt. You said you wanted to go back and sit in it. She dried her hands on the towel. I never did get that man's name.

Mom. Can I have this? I want it. She heard herself say it. Not for Vern. Not for the board. Rhonda looked at the picture in her hand, then at her. Kitty, it's been yours since you were seven. I was just keeping it on the fridge. Then Kit told her whose hand that was. Vern Pruett. He was the navigator. He's the one teaching me.

After the dishes she took her phone out on the back step, the one with the crack she'd put in it on roller skates in third grade, and called him. He picked up on the first ring, the way her mother did, and didn't bother with hello.
It was me. In your seat. Your ring's in the picture.
Nothing on the line a while but his television down the hall, the Royals, and Patrice telling the umpire what she thought. Then he cleared his throat.
Keep it that way, Sergeant. He hung up before she could think what to say back. She sat a minute longer with the phone in her lap, listening to a car go over the bridge.

Inside, her mother had wrapped half the roast in foil for Graham and written on it in cafeteria marker, GRAHAM, 350, 20 MIN, as if he'd never warmed up a roast in his life. The picture lay face up by her cup.

Her mother went in the drawer by the stove for a quart freezer bag. In went the picture. Out went the air, the way she did the buns on Fridays. She zipped it. Then she handed it across. Seven years old. Green shirt. Too big a seat. Looking up. She didn't put it in her coat. She carried it out to the truck in her hand, the way you'd carry something you meant to show somebody.
